source.title: PII Jailbreaking in LLMs via Activation Steering Reveals Personal Information Leakage
source.authors: K. K. Nakka; Xue Jiang; Dmitrii Usynin; Xue-Bing Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports activation steering and privacy-refusal results, but it does not test the listed claims about harmful or benign fine-tuning, response-position KL, compliant opening tokens, safety-localized weights, why safety is shallow, or deepening safety.
record.gate_note: The tested prompts ask about public figures' sexual orientation, and the intervention modifies attention activations at inference time. This is not a test of the listed harmful-request or token-depth claims. Rows below record related privacy-refusal results as none. No fine-tuning, token-position KL, prefilling, suffix, decoding-change, weight-edit, or safety-deepening result is reported.
record.test_reason: The study steers attention-head activations at inference time to turn privacy refusals about public figures' sexual orientation into disclosures. It does no fine-tuning, so V1 and V2 are untested. It measures no per-position KL (V3). It uses no prefilling, suffix or decoding change (V4). It does no weight or rank localization (V5). It does no analysis of causes (V6) and no deepening training (V7). Qi et al. (2310.03693) appears only in related work, as an example of harmful fine-tuning jailbreaks. Probe-guided activation steering is a related but different intervention, so its findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that steering refusal-predictive attention heads bypasses privacy refusal (at least 80% disclosure, best of 66 configurations) and can surface factual memorised personal information. They call for more rigorous privacy testing.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses inference-time, probe-guided activation steering on privacy queries. It does not apply the cited harmful fine-tuning method or measure first-token concentration.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering strength α and number of selected heads k affect the number of successful disclosures; the effective parameter combinations occupy a limited region, and the optimum varies by model.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes on last-prompt-token attention-head activations predict privacy refusal versus disclosure. The best Llama2-7B head has AUC-ROC 0.89 and F1 0.83, and middle layers are most predictive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Privacy-refusal behaviour is linearly decodable from mid-layer attention-head activations before generation.

fits_no_version.finding: Probe-guided steering of top-k heads yields at least one response labelled disclosed for 81.6%, 96.0% and 80.3% of initially non-disclosing subjects (Llama2-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, GLM-4). This is a best-of-66 measure across steering configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time activation steering at a small set of attention heads bypasses privacy refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Among jailbroken subjects, GPT-4o-mini rated steered responses factual at least once for 68.8% to 89.9%. Only 10 factual cases per model were checked by hand.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering-induced privacy disclosures can reveal memorised true personal information.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Trustworthy NLP (TrustNLP 2026)
record.problems: Factuality is first assessed by an LLM evaluator; only 10 cases were manually validated. The study covers one private attribute, and the authors report disagreements among human annotators on disclosure labels. The paper inconsistently names the GLM model size, and reports Qwen's steering rate as 96.0% in Table 2 but 96.1% in the prose.
record.rows_left_out: Probe results for other models and the layer-wise probe plots in Figures 5 and 7 are not separately tabulated in the text and are not extracted as numeric rows.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
No prefilling of a compliant start, no adversarial suffixes, no decoding changes. The intervention is activation addition at the last prompt token.
No weight or rank localization. Steering a top-k subset of heads (k from 16 to 96) is an activation intervention, and no ablation of weights is reported.
No analysis of why safety is shallow.
No deepening training or robustness test of it.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the relation from 'discusses' to 'cites_only', because the paper's only contact with the claim is a related-work citation of Qi et al. The record's peer_reviewed field ('TrustNLP 2026') is not supported by the text, which shows only the arXiv v2 of Aug 2025, so it should be verified. The jailbreak rates are best-of-66 configurations on subjects selected for non-disclosure, so they are not comparable to single-attack success rates. Figure 2 baseline disclosure rates for seven models (1.5% to 84%) are not extracted, but they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning or harmful-request compliance test.
No benign-data fine-tuning or resulting harmful-compliance test.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
No compliant-start prefilling, suffix, or decoding-change test; inference-time activation steering is a different intervention.
No test that safety is carried by a small set of weights or ranks; probe-guided activation steering is not a weight or rank localization test.
No test of whether training data or objective produces shallow safety.
No training to deepen safety or evaluation of whether deepened safety holds up.

rows.note: The paper also reports F1 0.83 for this best-performing probe; the result concerns prediction of privacy responses, not the listed safety-localization claim.
